author: @wladimirb1506
comment:
Leased a 2026 Hyundai Tucson N-Line X 1.6 150 hp FWD petrol since 11/25, driven 3,000 km so far:

Pros: great design, excellent interior quality (N-Line), lots of space, good acceleration, top-notch infotainment, strong matrix headlights, very good Krell sound system, comfortable seats, and the panoramic roof is a nice touch. The suspension feels nicely agile without being floaty, yet still very composed on rough roads.

Cons: fuel consumption is higher than expected: around 9 l/100 km mixed, 6.0 l/100 km is possible at 100 km/h, but on longer motorway trips at 130 km/h it’s hardly ever below 8.5 l/100 km. The lane-keeping assist keeps the car too far to the left, which feels uncomfortable. The automatic transmission reacts slowly: shifting from D to R feels like it takes 1.5–2 seconds, and when pulling away there’s first a short delay, then a sudden, jerky surge of power. The throttle is also tuned very aggressively in the 0–20 km/h range. Maybe it will improve as the system adapts, but right now it still feels rather poor.

Conclusion: I would choose it again. For me, the overall balance works.

video_title: Best Compact Car: 8-Car Mega Comparison
author: @jneedee
comment: Wow. As someone who is a DIYer and recently lost 10Gs on a bad Honda engine design, I'd like to expand a bit on these results... A car is much more than it's electronic gadgets, which in reality, creates really lazy and bad habits. Of ALL of the vehicles tested here, I find it misrepresentative of reality that the Nissan ends last in this test. It is the least gadgety and subjectively one of the top 2 best looking of the bunch. I recently test drove most of these vehicles and they all have jarring unexpected issues. Especially the lag on the VW and the crummy fabric inside the Honda. What's also surprising is that the Kia and the Hyundai finish so far apart given they practically the SAME vehicle at base. There is a lot of whine about how the Nissan falls behind on tech. Tech though, isn't trying to reconnect your phone multiple times or having so little adjustability in the driver assist controls. I think these are much more a nuisance and considerably more prone to issues than simply driving like a responsible citizen. Especially the cost when something goes wrong... And running costs is a HUGE consideration when you're rating on essentially what are "economy" minded vehicles. Any Turbo, no matter the recommendations, need to run on premium fuel in order to avoid issues - especially with the now common direct injection engines that build up carbon like nobody's business. And this adds a massive 35-50% to the cost of fuel alone, let alone the eventual Turbo rebuild. Essentially there are so many real world factors that go unconsidered in this comparison that it is unhelpful in any real way, and potentially misleading in others. I do however enjoy the in camera performance of the assessors. So thanks for that.

author: @cycletarmac
comment:
What a stupid comparison.  The civid hybrid is so much more expensive than most of the rest.  Compare a gas model Civic against the rest.  Another commenter was right, if you are adding the hybrid Civic to the comparison you need to add the si and GLI.

I've had 5 civics since 1995 up to 2018 and each time the quality dropped.  Bad quality brakes, engine problems, power steering rack failure and now an elevated price with no deals to be had.  Since then I had a 2019 GLI and the 2022 Jetta and now a 2026 Impreza RS.  I've had over 20 vehicles since 1995 so more than the average person.  Here are the highlights.

- 1995 Civic in manual lasted 180k km but did have engine gasket issues but that was at the end and I pushed that egine hard and never replaced the clutch.
- Used 2008 V6 Sport Rav4.  Had it for 5 years after I bought it used and put about 70k km.  No problems other than failing sunroof.  In the end the back seat was just too uncomfortable (seats too low) as the kids got bigger.
- 2007 Subaru Impreza: this was a tank in manual transmission.  Tried to get stuck in the snow but couldn't.   Not sure why I got rid of it to be honest.
- 2021 Tiguan - still have this and out of all the family size vehicles that I had (2001 Outback, 2007 Pilot, 2008 Odyssey, 2011 Forester, 2008 Rav4, 2017 Highlander, 2018 Santa Fe) the Tiguan is the Goldilocks of the group when considering space, power, handling, price, styling).  Luckily I had warranty for engine repair so we'll see how much lo ger I keep it considering powertrain warranty ends in August 2026.  This has been my favourit family hauler.
- 2019 GLI which I bought in 2021.   Felt fast when I first bought it and was fun to drive in manual.  Shifter was quite clunky until it warmed up in the winter and really poor traction even with winters.  Traded this in for a 2022 Jetta because the used market prices were crazy high and I got 8k more than I paid for my GLI one year later.   2022 Jetta had for 3 years and was on its 3rd set of rear brakes.  Sun glasses compartment failure (same as the tiguan) and steering  wheel had to be replace because of faulty sensors.  Really poor quality car and cheap radio and suspension. 
-2026 Subaru Impreza RS (Citron Yellow) - Traded in the leased 2002 Jetta and got $3300 in equit out of a car I put no money down on.  Early days but can without a doubt saythe best handling vehicle I have ever had.  The CVT surprising responsive  - doesntmake me miss my GLI.  Paddle shifters actually do something and "shifting" down actually slows down the vehicle similar to a manual where you often dont need to brake - unlike other brands that have 'manual mode' that just make the engine louder - talking about you Hyundai.

In the end,  Civics are not as good as they used to be and Honda is relying on past reputation.  They aren't bad cars but they don't justify their crazy prices nor fiance rates.  There are better cars out there with better deals to be had.  

I'm paying $380 taxes in on a Impreza RS lease.  Tell me where you can find a car of this quality for that price today  - CDN dollars.

comment:
This is a great video with wonderful information, but the AI "narrator" is off on some things (IN-teh-gra - nope In-TEH-gra). I also wouldn't call an I-4 engine in such surplatives, unless the car really deserves it (e.g., close to 400hp, 350 lb/ft). the turbocharged inline 4 is in most small cars - and, sadly more in mid-sized cars.

The Audi RS series is interesting: regardless of the model (RS3, RS4, RS5, RS7...) they all have comparable numbers. 0-60? Around 3.5 seconds (thanks to amazing engines mostly shipped from the Porsche factory in Stuttgart and the rally-tried Quattro AWD). Top Speed? About 175mph. But, hands down, they have been the most exciting cars that I can afford to drive (and service). To note: the RS5 has the same 2.9l V6 that's in the Porsche Cayenne S and Panamera S, but Audi tuned it up, raising the 375hp to 444hp for the RS5.

And I don't think the Mercedes C63 is powered by a 4-cylinder. I think it has the hand-built biturbo V8 that is standard in all AMG 63 series. The price tag helps explain the difference between the C53 and the C63 (or C63S).

comment: I'm one of those that believe a muscle car is basically an American car that has a high horsepower high torque V8 under the hood. Originally there was a difference between a true muscle car and a pony car, mainly the engine size and HP output. Also the size of the car. Muscle cars were bigger and had bigger engines and more HP. That changed in the latter part of the 60s and very early 70s when they started putting big blocks in pony cars which made them also muscle cars. Even the corvette sports car got big block power making it also a muscle car. The lines got blurred. Pony cars and even a sports car became muscle cars while also still being pony cars and a sports car. Today the lines are still blurred. Even though today's pony cars have mostly all small block motors they're putting out insane amounts of power with superchargers, turbos, nitrous, etc. Lots of V8 horsepower and torque is what makes any American car a muscle car in my book. Not everyone agrees and that's OK. But today's American performance cars have multiple labels. Pony cars, muscle cars, sports cars, sport sedans, and the new Corvette C8 and Ford GT are arguably super cars. Call it what you want, just drive it like you stole it

comment:
Okay okay okay, I don't think many people will agree with me, but hear me out here.

I own a final model ford falcon, XR6, it's a sport ute with a stick shift. Fun as, not particularly fast though. No turbo, but may boost her in the future.

I consider it to be a pony car since other falcons (XR8, GT-F, Pursuit ute, so on) have big Barra and Boss V8 motors under the hood, and my ute is like the baby brother of those bigger muscle cars.

As I said, mine is not by any means a beast. It pumps out about 195kw (261hp) and 391nm of torque from a 4.0L straight six. Rear drive too, baby.

Turbo ones were available from factory, however I am a new-ish driver on my second year of a probationary licence, and am not yet legally allowed to own a car that puts out (I believe) 300+ hp. So no turbo for me yet.

I bought it at a fairly chunky sum for someone my age, but being a ute, I have access to the HUGE back tray and it's still sporty enough to rip around twisties when I want to. If you're so inclined, yes, you can easily kick the back end out. The low end torque is very good with this motor.

I will probably move on to a more powerful vehicle after paying this one off, sure, but for the time being, I see it as a pony (or sports) car, and a nod of respect to its turbo six and V8 variants.

I get a bit of crap for what bought it for, being a naturally aspirated six, but I wish that weren't the case. I'm as much of a driver and an enthusiast as the next person. I love the falcon platform.

In my eyes, my ute is a little slice of the bigger musclebois and thus, a pony car.
